title: Annotated Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices
author: Personally transmitted by the Patriarch Bodhidharma
excerpt: 'The Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices,' personally transmitted by the Patriarch Bodhidharma to Daoyu and Huike as the essential teaching on entering the Way, was recorded by the disciple Tanlin. This treatise is concise in words yet rich in meaning, complete in both principle and practice - truly the outline of the school and a guide for practitioners.

inline.s: Course
Textbook
Annotated by Zhanran

The Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices' is the essential teaching on entering the Way personally transmitted by the Patriarch Bodhidharma to Daoyu and Huike, recorded by the disciple Tanlin. This treatise is concise in words yet rich in meaning, complete in both principle and practice, truly the outline of the school and a guide for practitioners.

[Entering the Way] Realizing and entering the undefiled noble path. [Undefiled] Pure and free of afflictions. Outflow is another name for affliction, with the sense of leaking out: the afflictions of greed and hatred flow out ceaselessly day and night through the six sense gates (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind), and so they are called outflows. Also, outflow has the sense of falling; afflictions cause one to fall into the three evil paths (hell, hungry ghosts, animals), and so they are called outflows. One with afflictions is said to be with outflows; one free of afflictions is said to be without outflows. [The Two Entries and Four Practices] The two entries: the entry of principle and the entry of practice. The four practices: the practice of requiting injuries, the practice of following conditions, the practice of seeking nothing, and the practice of conforming to Dharma. [Daoyu, Huike] Daoyu and Huike were two of the four great disciples of the Patriarch Bodhidharma. Huike received Bodhidharma's robe and bowl and became the second patriarch of Chan. When the Patriarch Bodhidharma was about to leave, he left this message: 'My disciples number in the thousands; of those who have truly obtained my Dharma, only Huike has obtained the marrow, Daoyu the bones, the nun Zongchi the flesh, and Daofu the skin.'
Tanlin

[The Master was a man of the Southern Indian region of the western lands, of the brahmin caste, the third son of a king. His spiritual wisdom was open and bright; whatever he heard he understood. His resolve was set on the Mahayana path, and so he left the lay life and followed the black-robed monks, carrying on and exalting the holy lineage. His mind was deep, empty, and still, and he clearly discerned the affairs of the world; within and without were both clear to him, and his virtue surpassed the world.]

Master Bodhidharma was a man of the Southern Indian region of the western lands, of the brahmin nobility, the third son of a king. His gifts were extremely high; broad and open-minded, he understood upon a single hearing. Because his resolve was set on the Mahayana, he left the world to become a monk and inherited and spread the mind-teaching of Chan. With false thoughts exhausted and mind clear, he thoroughly discerned the affairs of this world; worldly dharmas and transcendental dharmas were both fully penetrated by him, and his virtue far surpassed the worldly sphere.
[Tanlin] A monk of the Sui dynasty, a disciple of Bodhidharma, the first patriarch of Chan. From the first year of the Yuanxiang era of the Northern Wei (
) to the first year of the Wuding era (

), he served as the recording scribe for the translation work of such masters as Gautama Prajnaruci, Vimoksasena, Bodhiruci, Buddhasanta, and others, and wrote prefaces. [Recording scribe] At the translation hall, one who takes down the translator's words in writing in Chinese. [Bodhidharma] Bodhidharma, the third son of the King of Fragrance of South India, mastered both the Mahayana and Hinayana Dharma, and was the twenty-eighth patriarch of Chan in India (ancient India). Sensing that the conditions in the eastern land were ripening, he came to China to spread the teaching; at the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty he crossed the sea and reached Guangzhou, and the emperor welcomed him to Jianye (present-day Nanjing). His conversation with the emperor was ill-matched, so he crossed the Yangtze into the Wei domain, and at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song he faced a wall for nine years, transmitting the mind-teaching of Chan to Huike, becoming the founding patriarch of Chinese Chan. Seeing that Buddhist practitioners in China mostly approached from the written word, and that the preaching masters likewise mostly explained the meaning in accordance with the text without practicing in earnest, not grasping the wondrous import of the scriptures, he therefore founded a unique school: not establishing words, seeing the mind and realizing the nature, and realizing the nature to become a Buddha. [Brahmin] One of the four castes of India, a clan that serves the great Brahma heaven and cultivates the pure conduct. [Western lands] Generally refers to the countries west of China, but specifically to India. [Southern India] The southern part of India. [Mahayana] An abbreviation of Maha-yana, translated into Chinese as the Great Vehicle. [Black and white ones] Zi is black and su is white; monks wear black robes and lay people generally wear white, so monks and laypeople are together called the black and white ones. [Carry on and exalt] To inherit and develop. [Holy seed] Awakening to the fact that all dharmas arise from false thoughts, and contemplating this deluded mind as being like empty space; cultivating thus, not clinging to any dharmas, being able to become the seed of the noble fruit - this is called the holy seed.

[Grieving that in the border lands the orthodox teaching had declined, he was able to travel far over mountains and seas to teach in the Han and Wei domains. Those who had put to rest the mind all turned to him in faith; those who clung to views instead slandered him. At that time there were only Daoyu and Huike, these two monks who, though young in years, were of outstanding will and lofty aspiration. Happening upon the Master, they attended on him for several years, respectfully and earnestly seeking instruction, and well received his intentions.]

Because he grieved over the decline of the orthodox teaching of the Buddha-Dharma in the border land (referring to China), he did not shrink from hardship but traveled far over high mountains and great seas to teach in China. Those who cultivated the mind all took refuge in him in faith; but those who held biased views slandered and reviled him. At that time there were only Daoyu and Huike, these two monks who, though young, were of outstanding intelligence and lofty aspiration. Happening upon the Master, they attended on him for several years, reverently and earnestly seeking instruction, and were skilled in grasping the Master's intent.

[Border land] The border regions. At that time Buddhism was centered in India, and places far from India were called border lands. [Decline] Decay and decline. [Han and Wei] 'Han' refers to China, and 'Wei' to the Northern Wei of the Northern and Southern dynasties period. The Patriarch Bodhidharma sailed to Guangzhou, and Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty welcomed him to Jianye, the capital of the southern dynasty. Their interview was ill-matched, so he crossed the river on a single reed and went north to Luoyang, the capital of the Northern Wei. Later he settled (resided) at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song, faced a wall for nine years, and transmitted the robe and bowl to Huike. [Putting to rest the mind] Entering the state of no-mind. The Essential Methods of the Transmission of Mind says:

'Apart from all marks, sentient beings and all Buddhas are not at all different; only when one can be without mind is that the ultimate. A student of the path, if he is not immediately without mind, though he cultivate through many eons will never accomplish the path, being bound by the practices of the three vehicles and unable to gain liberation.'

[The Master was moved by their sincerity and taught them the true Way. He had them thus settle the mind, thus put forth practice, thus conform to circumstances, and thus employ expedient means. This is the Mahayana method of settling the mind, causing there to be no error.]

Master Bodhidharma was moved by their sincerity and transmitted the true Way to them. He taught them thus to settle the mind, thus to put forth practice, thus to conform to circumstances, and thus to employ expedient means. He also told them that this is the Mahayana method of settling the mind; cultivating in accordance with it, one will not fall into error.

[Thus to settle the mind: wall contemplation. Thus to put forth practice: the four practices. Thus to conform to circumstances: guarding against ridicule and suspicion. Thus to employ expedient means: dispatching what is not clung to.]

Thus to settle the mind: wall contemplation. Thus to put forth practice: the four practices. Thus to conform to circumstances: guarding against ridicule and suspicion (not being moved in mind by ridicule and suspicion). Thus to employ expedient means: dispensing with clinging (not clinging to marks).
As for wall contemplation, the four practices, and the like, see the annotations in the main text.
[This briefly tells of the occasions that gave rise to it - that is all.]
The above
is but a brief account of the origin of this treatise.
[Yun er] That is all.
Note: The headings in the text were added by the annotator.
[Now, there are many paths to entering the Way; to state them concisely, they do not go beyond two kinds. The first is the entry of principle; the second is the entry of practice.]
The concrete practices for entering the bodhi path are many and various. But summarized, they are nothing other than these two aspects: the entry of principle and the entry of practice.
[Fu] A particle at the opening of a classical sentence. [Entering the Way] Entering the bodhi path. [Ultimate truth] The ultimate truth, that is, the real mark of all dharmas. The Buddha says:

'All dharmas are false and unreal; where they cease is called real, called the real mark, called the Dharma realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the truth of the ultimate meaning, called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning.'
(The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
volume forty,
the Kaundinya chapter.)

The entry of principle is to awaken to the principle and see the nature, clarifying the ultimate truth; the entry of practice is to pass through circumstances and eliminate habitual tendencies, realizing the ultimate truth. The entry of principle sees the nature; the entry of practice maintains it. The entry of principle gives rise to wisdom; the entry of practice removes obstructions. On the correct bodhi path, principle guides practice, and practice perfects principle.
[Maintaining] Still the mind to unite with the Way, so that practice and understanding correspond, and secretly guard it - this is called maintaining.

[By the entry of principle is meant: relying on the teachings to awaken to the essential source, deeply believing that all living beings share the same true nature, which is only covered over by the passing dust of delusion and so cannot be brought to light. If one abandons the false and returns to the true, stilling the mind in wall contemplation, with no self and no other, ordinary and sage alike as one, firmly abiding without shifting, no longer following the written teachings - this is to be in hidden accord with the principle, without discrimination, still and non-active; this is called the entry of principle.]

So-called entry of principle means relying on the scriptural teachings to awaken to and illuminate the essential source of the Buddha-Dharma, deeply believing that all sentient beings share the same true nature, which is only covered by afflictions (passing dust) and so cannot appear. If one wishes to remove deluded confusion and return to the true nature, one should still the spirit and quiet reflection and practice wall contemplation: erasing dualistic opposites, no self and no other, ordinary and sage alike as one - thus firmly abiding without shifting, no longer pondering phrases and doctrinal words (when practice arises, understanding ceases). Thus one is in silent accord with the principle, entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision, adverting toward the state of 'without discrimination, still and non-active'; this is called the entry of principle.

[Living beings] Creatures that contain life, that is, sentient beings. [True nature] Not false is called true; unchanging is called nature. It is the pure mind-essence originally possessed by us. The Surangama Sutra says:
'The false perceptions of the preceding sense-dust delude your true nature.'

[Passing dust] A metaphor for afflictions. Afflictions are not inherent to the mind-nature, so they are likened to a guest; afflictions are what defile the mind-nature, so they are likened to dust. [Still abiding] To concentrate the spirit and quiet reflection. [Wall contemplation] So-called wall contemplation refers to the contemplation practice of 'the mind like a wall, giving rise to no discrimination.' Master Guifeng says:

'Bodhidharma taught people to settle the mind by wall contemplation, saying: "Outwardly still all conditions, inwardly the mind no longer gasps; the mind like a wall - with this one can enter the Way." Is this not exactly the method of sitting meditation?'

(From the Preface to the Collection of the Various Commentaries on the Sources of Chan.) Thus, the essential point of 'wall contemplation' is to let no dharmas enter, giving rise to no discrimination; it does not mean facing a wall in sitting meditation. [No self and no other, ordinary and sage alike as one] Erasing dualistic opposition, ordinary beings and sages are not different (this is spoken in terms of the real mark). The Third Patriarch Sengcan's Inscription on Faith in Mind says:

'The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. Just have no hate and no love, and it is clearly revealed. With even a hair's breadth of difference, heaven and earth are set apart.'

(Translation: The supreme, wondrous Way is not difficult; the difficulty lies in one's own discriminating mind. Only when there is no hate and no love is the supreme Way clearly revealed. If there is even the slightest thought of hate or love, one is as far from the supreme Way as heaven is from earth.) Master Guifeng says:

'If one suddenly awakens to the fact that one's own mind is originally pure, fundamentally without afflictions, and that the undefiled wisdom-nature is originally complete in itself - this mind is the Buddha, ultimately not different - then to cultivate in accordance with this is the supreme vehicle of Chan, also called the Tathagata's pure Chan, also called the one-action samādhi, also called the thusness samādhi. This is the root of all samādhis; if one can cultivate it thought after thought, one naturally and gradually attains hundreds and thousands of samādhis. What has been handed down successively within the gate of Bodhidharma is this Chan.'
(The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era.)

Still abiding in wall contemplation', this is the initial handhold of the entry of principle - stilling delusion and cultivating the mind, directly entering prajñā. 'Wall contemplation' - the mind like a wall, giving rise to no discrimination. The Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted to Huike, saying:
'Outwardly still all conditions, inwardly the mind no longer gasps; the mind like a wall - with this one can enter the Way.'
The Essential Methods of the Transmission of Mind says:
'The mind like a stubborn rock, with no gap or crevice at all; all dharmas cannot penetrate into your mind, utterly without clinging - only then is there a small measure of accord.'
Master Baizhang says:

'Things of this world and beyond, all dharmas - do not remember them, do not think of them. Let go of body and mind, giving them ease. The mind like wood or stone, without discrimination. The mind doing nothing, and the ground of the mind as if empty; then the sun of wisdom naturally appears, like clouds parting and the sun coming out.'
(The Essentials of the Five Lamps.)

'Outwardly still all conditions, inwardly the mind no longer gasps; the mind like a wall - with this one can enter the Way' means: outwardly, still the clinging to conditions; inwardly, the mind gives rise to no thought; the mind, like a wall, gives rise to no discrimination - that is to say, objects cannot move the mind; thus one can enter the Way. Of these four phrases, the last is the fruit; the effort is done only in the first three.
Therefore, the essential point of entering the Way is:
outwardly still all conditions, inwardly the mind no longer gasps, the mind like a wall
. In the Treasury of the Buddha-dharma Sutra, the Buddha says:
'The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is without thinking and without thought.'
In the Surangama Sutra, the Buddha says:

'All sentient beings, from beginningsless time, in the continuity of birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind as the pure and bright essence of the nature, employ a multitude of false thoughts; these thoughts are not true, and therefore there is transmigration.'
The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says:
'That which is apart from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space.'
The Essential Methods of the Transmission of Mind says:
'Still thought and forget deliberation, and the Buddha himself appears before you.'
The Sixth Patriarch says:

'If you wish to know the essential of the mind, simply do not think about any good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-essence, serene and ever still, with wondrous functions like the sands of the Ganges.'
(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch.)
The White Cloud Essential of the Mind (The Precious Casket of Mind Contemplation)
says:

'Q: How does one see the mind and realize the nature? A: Bodhidharma's three phrases, "outwardly still all conditions, inwardly the mind no longer gasps, the mind like a wall," sum up everything. The Sixth Patriarch's "do not think of good, do not think of evil" is exactly "outwardly still all conditions." "Precisely at such a time" is exactly "inwardly the mind no longer gasps." Though the phrases differ, how could there be two truths? When one reaches "precisely at such a time," it is only one flavor of unmoving; sustaining this in a single thought through ten thousand years, what further Dharma could there be? "Which
(na, that is, which)

one is the original face of the Venerable Ming?' is a question phrase, called 'striking the trigger.' (In the Buddha-Dharma the mind is the trigger, so it is said: in a single thought returning to the trigger, one is the same as that originally obtained.) The school says: The ordinary man's mysterious gate is shut tight, and the lock of consciousness is hard to open. The trigger is the mysterious gate; the adept plants a single word on it, striking and setting off its trigger, and that person is suddenly awakened. Yet the most important thing in this gongan is the three words 'at such a time' (that is, the time of not thinking of good and evil), which is the secret of the Chan school. If one who has aroused the resolve can dwell the mind like this, then awakening is not far away. The patriarch says: 'At such a time, this is called the time before the Buddha was born.' Again it is called: 'Dwelling at the summit, of incomparable preciousness.' If in one day one can dwell the mind like this for several hours, only then does it accord with the Dharma. There is naturally an occasion for striking the trigger; one need not be guided by another. The patriarch says: 'Only be able to be at such a time, and do not worry that you will not attain thorough awakening.' This belongs to the secret essentials of the mind-method and can be practiced with effort.'

When adverse circumstances or favorable circumstances arrive, how should one interpret them and how should one deal with them? This is of crucial importance, because circumstances are transformed by the mind. In this treatise the Patriarch Bodhidharma uses the 'four practices' to interpret and to deal with them, in order to counteract the mark-clinging afflictive tendencies of love and hate, grasping and rejecting, and so forth that have existed since beginnings time, so as to attain the ultimate liberation of benefiting oneself and benefiting others.

[By the entry of practice is meant the four practices. All other practices are entirely gathered within these. What are the four? First, the practice of requiting injuries; second, the practice of following conditions; third, the practice of seeking nothing; fourth, the practice of conforming to Dharma.]

So-called entry of practice means the four practices; all other practices are entirely gathered within these four. What are the four? They are: First, the practice of requiting injuries: toward adverse circumstances, not generating hatred or aversion, but realizing the requital of wrongs and advancing on the path. Second, the practice of following conditions: toward favorable circumstances, not generating greed or attachment, but following conditions and conforming to the path. Third, the practice of seeking nothing: all seeking is suffering, so one abandons desire and becomes still, clinging to nothing. Fourth, the practice of conforming to Dharma: understanding that all dharmas are empty, so that the six perfections, the myriad practices, and the gathering and transforming of sentient beings are all without clinging to marks.

[Six perfections] The six practices that are the gateways by which one can cross from this shore of birth-and-death and suffering to the other shore of nirvāṇa's peace and bliss. They are: giving, precept-keeping, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajñā. Giving can ferry over stinginess and greed; precept-keeping can ferry over transgression; patience can ferry over anger; vigor can ferry over indolence; meditation can ferry over distraction; prajñā can ferry over stupidity.]

The practice of requiting injuries: when adverse circumstances arrive, this is the ripening of the fruit of past evil, self-caused and self-received; therefore one meets suffering without sorrow, realizing the requital of wrongs and advancing on the path.
[The ripening of the fruit of past evil] The fruit of past calamity (having harmed others in the past) and evil karma maturing. 'Su' means past, previous; 'yang' means calamity, harm.

[First, what is called the practice of requiting injuries? It means that the practitioner, when undergoing suffering, should reflect within himself: I, in the countless eons of the past, abandoned the root and followed the branches, wandering through the various realms of existence, arousing much resentment and hatred, and offending and harming without limit.]

First, what is called the practice of requiting injuries? It means that the practitioner, when undergoing suffering, should think thus: I, in the countless eons of the past, abandoned the true and pursued the false, rising and sinking in the sea of suffering of the various realms of existence, arousing many thoughts of resentment and hatred, and offending and harming countless sentient beings.

[The practice of requiting injuries] 'Requiting injuries' means dealing with the karma of wrongs. Here 'requite' has the sense of repaying. 'Injury' means enmity, as in 'enemy' or 'karmic debt.' The practice of requiting injuries means how one should correctly deal with adverse circumstances, because adverse circumstances are the manifestation of one's own past calamities and evil karma. [The various realms of existence] Refers to the manifold differences of the deluded world. The karma produced by sentient beings, from causes giving rise to fruits, is real and not empty; it can be divided into three existences, four existences, seven existences, nine existences, twenty-five existences, and so on, collectively called the various realms of existence. Moreover, these various realms of existence are the sea of birth and death in which ordinary sentient beings rise and sink, hence they are called the sea of the various existences.

[Now, although I have not so offended, this is the ripening of the fruit of my past calamities and evil karma; it is not something heaven or man can inflict. Willingly I accept it, without any complaint or grievance. The scripture says: 'Meet suffering without sorrow.' Why? Because one has come to know how things truly are. When this mind arises, it accords with the principle; realizing the requital of wrongs, one advances on the path. Hence it is called the practice of requiting injuries.]

Now, although I no longer so offend, this state of suffering is the ripening of the fruit of my past calamities and evil karma, and it is not something heaven or others can inflict; therefore I willingly accept it, with no sense of grievance at all. The scripture says: 'Meet suffering without sorrow.' Why no sorrow? Because one has understood the cause of undergoing suffering. Thus, in adverse circumstances, whatever thoughts arise all accord with the principle; realizing that the retribution of suffering is self-caused, self-received, and empty and unreal, one thereby advances in the practice of the path. This is the practice of requiting injuries.

Cultivating the practice of requiting injuries not only means meeting suffering without sorrow, but also makes adverse circumstances into a strengthening condition - realizing the requital of wrongs and advancing on the path. If one does not cultivate this practice, then in a state of suffering one is bound to resent heaven and blame others, even returning an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. This not only subjects one to all the more torment, but also creates new karma that will again bring retribution - such a vicious cycle, sinking into the sea of suffering endlessly.

[A strengthening condition] When one dharma helps another dharma to progress upward, this dharma is the strengthening condition of the other dharma. If one can correctly deal with adverse circumstances and realize the requital of wrongs, advancing on the path, then adverse circumstances are one's own strengthening condition.]

Requiting injuries is to take the path as one's mind, repaying debts and clearing accounts. This is to travel along with the path, not only dissolving karma but also advancing on the path. If instead habitual tendencies take charge and a mind of anger arises, this is to travel against the path; the old debts are not yet settled, and new debts are added - instead of advancing, one retreats.

The practice of following conditions: when favorable circumstances arrive, this is what one's past good has evoked; when the conditions are exhausted they return to nothing; therefore one lets gain and loss follow conditions, unmoved in mind, not anticipating what comes, not clinging to what goes.

[Second, the practice of following conditions: sentient beings have no self and are turned by conditions and karma; suffering and pleasure are both received, all arising from conditions. If one obtains such things as excellent rewards and honors, these are evoked by one's past causes. Having now obtained them, when conditions are exhausted they return to nothing - what is there to rejoice in? Gain and loss come from the mind; the mind neither increases nor decreases; the wind of joy cannot move it, and it silently accords with the path. Hence it is called the practice of following conditions.]

Second, so-called ones who follow conditions: sentient beings have no mastery over themselves; all are turned by karma, and their suffering and pleasure all arise in accordance with causes and conditions. If one obtains such things as excellent rewards and honors, that is what one's past wholesome deeds evoked, and only now is one able to obtain it. Once the conditions are exhausted, these excellent rewards vanish like smoke, so what is there to rejoice in? So-called gain and loss are all false calculations of the cognitive mind; when the mind arises, dharmas arise. If the mind is not made happy or sorrowful by gain and loss, then the wind of circumstances that delights people cannot move you, and you are secretly in accord with the path. Such practice is called the practice of following conditions - what comes comes, what goes goes; an even mind, freely going with conditions.

[Unmoved by the wind of joy] The wind of circumstances has a wind of sorrow and a wind of joy. Among the eight winds, decline, slander, ridicule, and suffering are the wind of sorrow; gain, praise, honor, and pleasure are the wind of joy. For one without skill, both sorrow and joy move the mind. When the effort of realizing the requital of wrongs and advancing on the path has gained strength, the wind of sorrow already cannot easily move the mind, but the wind of joy is hard to guard against. Therefore at this time, one should be especially wary of the wind of joy. [The eight winds] Gain and loss, slander and praise, honor and ridicule, suffering and pleasure. Gain is things that delight one; loss is things that disappoint one; slander is being reviled behind one's back; praise is being commended behind one's back; honor is being commended to one's face; ridicule is being mocked to one's face; suffering is the various pains of body and mind; pleasure is the various delights of body and mind. These eight dharmas are the objects of the world's love and hate, and moreover they can stir up the mind; hence they are likened to the 'eight winds.'

If one does not cultivate the practice of following conditions, then in favorable circumstances one is full of fear and anxiety over losing what one has gained; one may even create evil karma to protect what one has gained or to expand it. This not only greatly diminishes one's excellent reward, but will also bring evil retribution. What is more serious is that the mind is no longer on the path; favorable circumstances become evil conditions, and the practice of the path instead declines. Worldly people regard fame, profit, and wealth as far too important, bringing suffering upon themselves. Therefore the practitioner should realize that all dharmas are empty, take the path as the mind, meet suffering without sorrow, encounter pleasure without joy, and let everything be as it is naturally; at all times one tests one's own skill by being unmoved by the eight winds. Everywhere and at all times are the examination grounds on the bodhi path. If sentient beings abandon clinging and attachment, they can awaken to their original face; traveling along with the path, they can attain the path.
The practice of seeking nothing: all seeking is suffering, and no-seeking is pleasure; all existence is empty, so one stills thought and seeks nothing.

[Third, the practice of seeking nothing: worldly people are always deluded, clinging greedily everywhere, and this is called seeking. The wise awaken to the real and, in principle, reverse the worldly; they settle the mind in non-action, and their actions follow the turning of conditions.]

Third, so-called ones who seek nothing: worldly people are always deluded by illusions, clinging greedily everywhere, and this is called 'seeking.' The wise clearly awaken to the true character of all dharmas and, in principle, reverse the worldly (the worldly all cling and all seek; the wise do the opposite, following principle, not clinging, not seeking); they do not cling, they settle the mind in non-action, and they act freely.

[All existence is empty, so there is nothing to wish for or delight in. Merit and darkness continually follow one another. The three realms are without peace, like a burning house. To have a body is all suffering - who, in gaining anything, could ever be at ease?]

They know that all existence is empty, so there is nothing to wish for or delight in. Merit and the darkness of delusion continually follow one another. (Clinging greedily everywhere, the mind is in the darkness of delusion; settling the mind in no-seeking is itself merit.) The three realms are without peace, like a burning house. To have a body is all suffering; who can be at ease because of obtaining something? (Even the First Emperor of Qin had to die, and because of his greed he suffered a bitter retribution - what then is there to be greedy for? Where are the generals and ministers of ancient and modern times today? A mound of overgrown grass, that is all.)
[All existence is empty] All things are illusions. All existence means all things.
The Diamond Sutra says:
'All marks whatsoever are false and unreal.'

[Having fully understood this, one therefore stills thought and seeks nothing amid the various existences. The scripture says: 'All seeking is suffering; no-seeking is pleasure.' One judges and knows that no-seeking is the true non-active practice of the path; this is called the practice of seeking nothing.]

Having penetrated this principle, one therefore stills thought and seeks nothing amid all things. The scripture says: 'All seeking is suffering; no-seeking is pleasure.' Thus it is asserted that no-seeking is the true practice of the path. Such practice is called the practice of seeking nothing.
The true character of the universe and of life is: all dharmas are empty, without existence, ungraspable; therefore the practitioner of the path goes freely with conditions. The Heart Sutra says:

'Because of having nothing attained, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñā-paramita, has no hindrance in mind. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; far removed from inverted dreams and thoughts, one reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.'

If one has something that one hopes for, then one has a mind of gain and loss. With a mind of gain and loss, one cannot go freely with conditions, but instead calculates and clings. Following one's own inclinations, the mind runs counter to the path, impure and unequal; this is the greatest obstacle to cultivating and realizing the fruit.

blocks.text: (4) The Practice of Conforming to Dharma

inline.s: The practice of conforming to Dharma: all existence is empty, so the six perfections, the myriad practices, and the gathering and transforming of sentient beings are all without clinging to marks; only this is practice that accords with the Dharma. Not clinging to marks means not endowing marks with any reality: 'not taking hold of marks, ever still, unmoving.'

[The practice of conforming to Dharma] Practice in accordance with the Dharma. Here 'conforming' means to accord with. The 'Dharma' here is as the passage below says: 'The principle of the pure nature is called Dharma. By this principle, all marks are empty, without defilement and without attachment, without this and without that.' The Diamond Sutra says:
'All marks whatsoever are false and unreal.' 'Not taking hold of marks, ever still, unmoving.'

[Fourth, the practice of conforming to Dharma: the principle of the pure nature is called Dharma. By this principle, all marks are empty, without defilement and without attachment, without this and without that. The scripture says: 'In the Dharma there are no sentient beings, because it is free of the defilement of sentient beings; in the Dharma there is no self, because it is free of the defilement of self.' If the wise can believe and understand this principle, they should practice in accordance with the Dharma.]

Fourth, so-called one who conforms to Dharma: the principle of the inherently pure self-nature is called Dharma. This principle says: all marks are empty, and the nature is serene, so the practitioner should be without defilement and without attachment, without this and without that. The scripture says:
'In the Dharma there are no sentient beings, because it is free of the mark of sentient beings; and there is no self, because it is free of the mark of self.'

(This means: the practitioner should be free of the mark of sentient beings and the mark of self, not making a distinction between self and other.) If a wise person can believe and understand this principle, then he should practice in accordance with the Dharma, not clinging to the mark of sentient beings and not clinging to the mark of self.

[All marks are empty] All marks are empty. 'Si' means 'is, are.' Example: 'With preparation there is no calamity.' [In the Dharma there are no sentient beings, because it is free of the defilement of sentient beings; in the Dharma there is no self, because it is free of the defilement of self] This is quoted from the Vimalakirti Sutra
the third chapter, on the disciples. In the scripture, the great Maudgalyayana says to the Buddha:

'I recall that in the past I entered the great city of Vaisali and in the lanes and alleys preached the Dharma to a gathering of laypeople. At that time, Vimalakirti came and said to me: "Look, Maudgalyayana! In preaching to the white-clad lay devotees, one should not be as you have spoken. One who preaches the Dharma should preach it in accordance with the Dharma. In the Dharma there are no sentient beings, because it is free of the defilement of sentient beings; in the Dharma there is no self, because it is free of the defilement of self."'

(Translation: I recall that in the past I entered the great city of Vaisali and in the lanes and alleys preached the Dharma to a gathering of laypeople. At that time, Vimalakirti came and said to me: Look, Maudgalyayana! In preaching to lay devotees, one should not be as you have spoken. In preaching to people, one must preach in accordance with the Dharma, speaking the real mark of all dharmas. In the Dharma there are no sentient beings, because it is free of the mark of sentient beings; and there is no self, because it is free of the mark of self.) [The defilement of sentient beings, the defilement of self] These are the mark of sentient beings and the mark of self. The mark of sentient beings and the mark of self arise from falsely clinging to the reality of sentient beings and self; these are the mind-defilements that obscure thusness. Therefore the mark of sentient beings and the mark of self are also called the defilement of sentient beings and the defilement of self. As for the principle of being free of the four marks (the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, the mark of a life), it is set forth in detail in the Diamond Sutra. In the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha says:
'If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, or the mark of a life, then he is no bodhisattva.'
(For the detailed annotation see
Annotated Diamond Sutra
[Lanes and alleys] Small streets and narrow alleys.

[The Dharma-body, without stinginess, practices giving of body, life, and wealth, with a mind without grudging. Fully understanding the three modes of emptiness, one neither leans on nor clings. Only to remove defilement and gather and transform sentient beings, without taking hold of marks. This is self-benefiting, and again able to benefit others, and also able to adorn the path of bodhi. As the perfection of giving is thus, so too are the other five. To remove false thinking, one cultivates the six perfections, yet practices nothing; this is the practice of conforming to Dharma.]

The practitioner is a body of principle (the Dharma-body), without stinginess or greed; one should give of one's own body, life, and wealth, with a mind without grudging. Fully understanding the threefold emptiness, one is neither partial nor attached. Only for removing the defilement of one's own mind and gathering and transforming sentient beings does one not take hold of marks. Thus it not only benefits oneself but also benefits others, and can also adorn the path of bodhi. Giving is like this, to be free of marks; the other five perfections are likewise to be free of marks. To remove false thinking, in cultivating the six perfections one practices without practice, the mind uniting with the path; this is called the practice of conforming to Dharma.

[Dharma-body] Refers to the appearance of one who is a renunciant wearing the Dharma robe. Here it means that the practitioner takes the Dharma as his body, not falsely clinging to the physical body. [To practice dana, giving] To practice giving. 'Dana' is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit word dana, translated into Chinese as 'giving.' 'To practice dana, giving' is a double expression in Sanskrit and Chinese. [Three modes of emptiness] The receiver, the giver, and the thing given, these three marks are all empty; this is also called the threefold emptiness. [The threefold emptiness] The 'three wheels' refer to the giver, the receiver, and the thing given; after giving, if these three wheels are not retained in the mind, it is called the threefold emptiness. [To remove false thinking, cultivate the six perfections, yet practice nothing] This means that the practice of the six perfections is one's own duty; the mind should be great in measure, without the mark of self, without the mark of sentient beings, to 'do without doing' - that is, having done it as if one had not done it, leaving not the slightest trace in the mind. Contrariwise, if one practices the six perfections and at the same time the mind clings to what is practiced, even becoming smug, thinking itself superior and letting thoughts run wild, that runs counter to the path. Therefore, to do good while the mind does not cling to the good, then whatever one accomplishes is complete. The Diamond Sutra says:

'Good men and good women who set their minds on anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should give rise to such a mind: I should extinguish and deliver all sentient beings; and yet, having extinguished and delivered all sentient beings, there is not a single sentient being that is really extinguished and delivered.'

The practice in accord with the Dharma means this: to practice the six perfections while abiding in no mark. Since the six perfections are led by charity, this passage takes charity as representing the six perfections; the remaining five are likewise, practicing while not practicing. The Diamond Sutra says:

“If a bodhisattva’s mind abides in the Dharma and so practices charity, it is like a man entering the darkness who sees nothing. If a bodhisattva’s mind does not abide in the Dharma and so practices charity, it is like a man with eyes, who in the bright light of the sun sees all kinds of forms.”

blocks.text: Appendix: The Patriarch Bodhidharma’s Method of Pacifying the Mind

inline.s: (From the Essentials of the United Lamp.)

In delusion the person pursues the Dharma; in awakening the Dharma pursues the person. In awakening consciousness encompasses form; in delusion form encompasses consciousness. Whatever involves a mind that discriminates and reckons the present measure of one’s own mind is wholly a dream; if one realizes the mind as quiescent and extinct, with no place for a single thought, this is called right enlightenment.
Question: What is the present measure of one’s own mind?

Answer: When one sees all dharmas as existing, their existence is not self-existing—it is one’s own mind that reckons them as existing. When one sees all dharmas as non-existent, their non-existence is not self-non-existent—it is one’s own mind that reckons them as non-existent. And so it is with all dharmas alike: they are all one’s own mind reckoning them as existing, one’s own mind reckoning them as non-existent. Moreover, if a person has committed all manner of offenses and within himself sees his own Dharma-king, he gains liberation. One who attains understanding from practical matters has vigorous power; one who sees the Dharma amid practical matters never loses mindfulness anywhere. One who understands from words and letters is weak in power; one who sees the Dharma right in the midst of things is deep. Whatever movements, leaping, and stumbling you may make, none go beyond the Dharma-realm. If one enters the Dharma-realm by means of the Dharma-realm, that is a fool. Every activity whatsoever does not go beyond the Dharma-realm mind. Why? Because the essence of the mind is the Dharma-realm.
Question: People in the world study all manner of learning; why do they not attain the Way?

Answer: Because they see a self, they do not attain the Way. “Self” means “I.” The sage meets suffering without sorrow and joy without delight, because he does not see a self and so does not know suffering or joy; because he has lost the self, he reaches emptiness. If the self is itself lost, what other thing is there that is not lost?
Question: Since all dharmas are empty, who cultivates the Way?

Answer: If there is a someone, then that someone needs to cultivate the Way; if there is no someone, then there is no need to cultivate. “Someone” is also “I.” If there is no self, then in encountering things no right and wrong arise. “Yes” is when I myself affirm it, yet the thing is not so; “no” is when I myself negate it, yet the thing is not not-so. In the very mind being without a mind—this is the thoroughgoing attainment of the Buddha-way; in things themselves giving rise to no views—this is called having reached the Way. When one encounters things and goes straight through, knowing their original source, this person’s eye of wisdom opens. The wise one lets things be and not the self, and so has no grasping or rejecting, no compliance or opposition; the foolish one lets the self be and not things, and so has grasping and rejecting, compliance and opposition. To see no single thing is called seeing the Way; to take no single thing as one’s practice is called practicing the Way. In every place there is no place; in that place of doing there is no place of doing, no Dharma-doing, and one sees the Buddha. If one sees marks, then in every place one sees ghosts. Because one grasps marks one falls into hell; because one contemplates the Dharma one gains liberation. If one sees recollections and discriminations, one incurs such things as the cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of coals, and directly sees the marks of birth and death. If one sees the nature of the Dharma-realm, that is the nature of nirvāṇa. Without recollection of marks and without discrimination, that is the nature of the Dharma-realm. The mind is not form, and so is not existent; it functions without ceasing, and so is not non-existent. Again, it functions yet is ever empty, and so is not existent; it is empty yet ever functions, and so is not non-existent.
